This ClearHire changelog is a high-level, honest record of the app's notable changes and the capabilities it ships today. It is intentionally brief and factual: it tracks what exists and broadly when, without precise day-level dates or invented version history. For how any single feature works, follow the links into the feature pages.

The rebuild reached Google Play as version 2.15.0 on 27 October 2026, and the web app serves the same release. Earlier notes called it 2.0.0: the number changed so that its middle figure matches the Android build number, and nothing else about the release changed with it. This version replaces the backend. Existing installs start from an empty account — data from earlier versions is not carried over. Export anything you need before updating. That sentence is the whole of what changed for anyone who used ClearHire before, and it is deliberate rather than a fault: 2.0 is a rebuild on a different database, and nothing was migrated across. What the rebuild changed under the surface: the product runs on Supabase — a Postgres database with row-level security — instead of Firestore. Every page was rebuilt against an approved design rather than ported, which is why some screens read differently even where the feature is the same. What is new to use: The phone app view — on a phone, ClearHire opens with a top bar, a tab bar and one action under your thumb (October 2026). Requesting a paid plan — Pro and Team are requested in the app and set up on your account by the ClearHire team (October 2026). Challenges, badges and levels with an opt-in leaderboard — and, to be clear about what is not there, no streaks. Points come from finishing something, never from opening the app. System announcements with three levels of loudness, one of which cannot be dismissed. Analytics covering where a profile view came from, how long each application stage has taken, and how each resume performs. A referral programme — an invite link, points and a badge on every confirmed referral. What was dropped: the browser extension is not part of ClearHire 2.0. It was never published, and the page explains what to use instead.

Version 1.12.x — 2026. The 1.12.x line was: a profile-driven resume builder, employment verification, job search and application tracking, mutual reviews, career tools, gamification, and analytics. The web app has run the rebuild since September 2026, and the Android app joined it with 2.15.0 on 27 October 2026. The Android app is live on Google Play, but the version installed there may trail the web app while an update is in review. The Play listing is the authoritative source for which Android version is currently published — check it there rather than assuming it matches this page. Some earlier version numbers (1.9.0 and 1.9.1) were prepared internally and never published at all, so they do not appear as releases here.

The current release added a few ways ClearHire keeps you informed, plus internal delivery improvements: In-app notifications for application-status changes, employment-verification results, reviews, and occasional admin announcements. Optional push notifications you can turn on in Notification Settings — off by default; the app works fully without them. A few transactional emails (welcome, contact-form reply, account-deletion confirmation, identity-verification result). No marketing email. Anonymous profile-view counting — profile views now include signed-out visitors, counted at most once per visitor per day. Over-the-air updates on Android so web-layer fixes can reach the installed app without waiting for a store release. There are three plans — Free, Pro and Team — and Free is a real plan rather than a trial. It covers building and exporting resumes, tracking applications, asking for employment verification, the career tools and the community, with limits on how many of some things you can hold at once. Pro and Team raise those limits; Team applies its limits to every seat in full rather than dividing them between seats. The current figures live on the pricing page in the app, which is the only place they are authoritative — a price copied into documentation is a price that goes stale without anybody noticing. ClearHire shows first-party promotions for the developer's other apps and uses no third-party ad networks. A separate paid white-label licence exists for organizations that want their own branded deployment; it has no effect on the public app. Supporting the project at aoneahsan.com/payment is optional and separate from any plan.

Yes. Because ClearHire saves your profile, resumes, applications, and verification requests, you sign in so your data persists and syncs across devices. Sign-in is Google-only — there is no email-and-password registration. If you do not want to use a Google account, ClearHire is not usable today.

Analytics in ClearHire is the feature that surfaces measurable signals from your job-search activity — such as profile views, resume downloads, and application progress — so you can see what is happening and adjust your approach. A job search produces a lot of activity that usually disappears; analytics keeps the useful parts visible.

Metric What it tells you Profile views How often your profile is being seen Resume downloads How many times your resume has been downloaded Application tracking Where your applications stand across stages

Profile views indicate visibility. A rising count suggests your profile is reaching more people; a flat count may be a cue to enrich your profile or broaden your job search. Profile views include signed-out visitors, not just people who are logged in. Each visitor is counted at most once per day using a per-visitor identifier and a server-side rule, so someone reloading your public profile cannot inflate the number. This makes the count a best-effort, approximate measure of reach — not a precise unique-visitor metric.
Resume downloads reflect tangible interest in your CV. Pair this with the resume builder and ATS checker to keep the resume people download as strong as possible.
Analytics works hand in hand with application tracking: seeing how applications move from applied toward offer helps you spot where you stall and where you convert.

Low profile views? Strengthen your profile and verify key roles via employment verification. Downloads but no progress? Tighten your resume and revisit your career tools prep. Stalling at a stage? Focus your effort where applications consistently drop off.

It does not identify exactly who viewed you beyond the signals ClearHire provides. The view count is approximate. Views are deduplicated per visitor per day on a best-effort basis, not tallied as precise unique visitors. It does not predict offers. Metrics describe activity; they do not forecast outcomes. It is not a vanity score. The point is to inform action, not to chase numbers for their own sake.

documents.t: Application tracking in ClearHire is the feature that organizes every job you apply to into clear stages — from applied through to offer — so you can see the status of each opportunity in one place. Instead of juggling spreadsheets, email threads, and memory, you log each application and move it along a pipeline as things progress.

A typical job hunt runs many applications at once, each at a different point. Tracking them as stages keeps the picture clear: Stage What it means Applied You submitted your application In review / screening The employer is reviewing Interview One or more interview rounds underway Offer An offer has been extended You advance each application as it moves, so your dashboard always reflects reality. The exact labels and flow follow the app, but the principle is a single pipeline from start to outcome.

Nothing slips. You know who you applied to and when, so follow-ups happen on time. You see momentum. A glance shows how many roles are active and where they stand. You prioritize. Time goes to the opportunities furthest along or most promising.

Find roles in job search, then log them here. Tailor and export a CV in the resume builder for each application. Review your activity in analytics, which can reflect application progress alongside profile views and resume downloads.

This page exists because it used to say the opposite, and a page that quietly disappears leaves anyone who bookmarked it or found it in a search result with no explanation.

documents.t: An earlier version of ClearHire had a desktop Chrome add-on in development. It captured a LinkedIn profile, auto-filled job-application forms on three sites, and kept a local list of jobs you had looked at. It was never published to any store. Nobody outside development ever installed it, and no data ever passed through it.

ClearHire was rebuilt in 2026, and the rebuild deliberately left the extension out of scope. The reasoning was narrow and worth stating plainly: an extension is a separate product with its own store review, its own permission model, its own update cycle and its own privacy surface. Bundling one into a web app's scope makes both later and neither better. That is a decision about ClearHire's scope, not a judgement that the idea is bad. If an extension is ever built, it will be announced as its own thing rather than reappearing quietly on this page.

documents.t: Everything the prototype did has a home in the app itself: Keeping track of where you applied — application tracking records the role, the company, the stage and what you sent, whether or not you applied through ClearHire. Checking a resume against a posting — the ATS resume checker does that in the browser, with no install.

documents.t: Company reviews in ClearHire are written assessments of employers that are connected to a verified employment relationship, so the people leaving feedback are those who genuinely worked there. The same mechanism runs in both directions: candidates review companies, and companies review employees. Because each review is tied to a verified employment link, the system favors accountability over anonymous, unconnected opinions.

The defining idea is mutuality grounded in a real relationship: A candidate who worked at a company can review that employer. A company can review an employee who worked there. Both sides connect to the same verified employment link, so reviews reflect an actual working relationship. This differs from open review sites where anyone can post about any company. Here, the connection between reviewer and reviewed is the foundation, which raises the signal of each review.

documents.t: As a job seeker: share your experience of an employer — culture, management, day-to-day reality — to help other candidates. Be specific and fair. Concrete observations help more than vague praise or complaints. Stick to your real experience. Reviews are tied to a relationship for a reason — keep them honest. Focus on what's useful to the other side. Future candidates and future employers are the audience.

They are not anonymous free-for-alls. Reviews are tied to verified employment, not posted by unconnected strangers. They are not a guarantee of accuracy. documents.t: Employment verification in ClearHire is the process by which a former or current employer confirms that a specific role on your profile is real, after which that role is countersigned. It is the feature that sets ClearHire apart from ordinary resume tools: instead of asking employers to take your claims on faith, the platform lets the other party to the employment relationship acknowledge it directly. Verification is per role, not per person. Confirming one job countersigns that one experience entry; other roles remain unconfirmed until a company answers for them too.

In your profile, open the experience entry you want verified. Start a verification request, identifying the employer or the contact who can confirm the role. The employer receives the request and reviews it on their side. If they confirm, the role is countersigned, which backs it across ClearHire. For a candidate-side, step-by-step walkthrough, see request employment verification.

On the company side, an authorized contact can confirm (or decline) the request through ClearHire for companies. Verification requests are not open forever: the employer-side request has a timeout. If the request is not actioned within that window, it lapses rather than lingering indefinitely. You can try again, reach out to the employer directly, or choose a different contact who can confirm the role. This timeout is deliberate. It keeps requests current and avoids a backlog of stale, unanswered asks. Silence expires the request instead of failing it, so a role with no countersignature is not false. It is unconfirmed, which is where every role starts.
documents.s: The employer side and the timeout

documents.t: A countersignature is a precise, narrow signal. Be honest about its scope when you rely on it. A countersignature confirms A countersignature does NOT confirm An employment relationship existed Your performance or how well you did the job The employer acknowledged the role Your exact salary or compensation The role on your profile is real The seniority implied by your title It was confirmed by the other party Anything about roles you did not verify In short: verification proves the relationship, not the rating. Treat it as proof of "this happened," not "this person was excellent."
documents.s: What a countersignature proves, and what it does not

documents.t: Because both company reviews and employee reviews in ClearHire are tied to a verified employment link, verification also underpins the platform's review system. Feedback comes from people who genuinely worked together, which is more meaningful than anonymous, unconnected reviews. A countersigned record gives each review a real basis.

Verify your most important roles first — the ones a hiring manager will scrutinize. Pick a contact who can actually confirm the role (HR or a direct manager), so the request does not time out unanswered. Re-request if it lapses. A timeout is not a rejection; you can send a fresh request. Keep claims honest. Verification only confirms reality, so describe roles accurately.

documents.t: ClearHire for companies is the employer side of the platform that lets organisations create company profiles, post jobs, manage applicants, search for talent, review employees, and confirm employment through verification. It is the counterpart to the job-seeker experience: where candidates build a record a company can countersign, companies post roles and engage with candidates whose claims can be confirmed.

Create one or more company profiles, each with its own office locations and branding — colors, banners, and taglines. A well-built profile gives candidates a clear sense of who you are and lets a single account manage several companies or business units.

Post roles with detailed requirements and salary ranges. Adding a salary range is not just good practice; it also feeds the candidate-side salary filter, helping the right applicants find your role. Clear requirements improve match quality and reduce noise in your pipeline.

Manage candidates through a hiring pipeline so you always know where each applicant stands. This mirrors the candidate's own application tracking from the other side: as you move people through stages, both you and the process stay organized. Capability What it does Company profiles Multiple companies, locations, and branding Job posting Requirements plus salary ranges Applicant tracking A pipeline to manage candidates Talent search Find people by skills, experience, and location Employee reviews Review employees tied to verified roles Verification Confirm employment for your employees

Search for candidates by skills, experience, and location to source proactively rather than waiting for applications. Combined with ClearHire's verification layer, you can engage candidates whose work history can be confirmed.

Either side can start it: a current or former employee can ask your company to confirm a role, or an authorised contact at your company can start the record. Confirmations are time-bound: requests carry a timeout, so action them promptly to avoid letting valid requests lapse. Confirming puts a named person at your company, with their own job title and the date, behind three facts: the job title, the company and the dates. See employment verification for how the request flow works end to end.

Reviews on ClearHire are mutual and tied to a verified employment link. As a company, you can review employees who genuinely worked with you, just as they can review you. This keeps feedback grounded in real relationships rather than anonymous posts — see company reviews.
Company insights help you understand engagement with your profile and postings, so you can refine how you present roles and your brand to candidates.

Verification is not a background check. Confirming a role acknowledges the relationship; it does not assess performance, salary, or conduct. Posting a job does not guarantee applicants. Clear requirements and salary ranges help, but reach depends on candidate activity. Talent search is bounded by the platform. You search candidates within ClearHire, not the entire labor market.

documents.t: ClearHire has a progression layer: challenges you can finish, badges that record that you did, levels that rise with your points, and a leaderboard you have to opt into. It exists to make the slow, invisible parts of a job search visible — a profile kept current, a record confirmed by a company, a question answered in the forums.

Points come from finishing a challenge, never from opening the app, and they are never removed. There is no streak to break and nothing decays. That is not a summary. It is the design's own sentence, and it rules out the two mechanics people most expect to find here. ClearHire has no streaks. Not a lapsed feature, not a planned one — they are a stated non-goal, because a counter that punishes you for a quiet week is measuring your attendance rather than your progress. Nothing you have earned can be taken away by not showing up.
documents.s: The one rule worth reading first

documents.t: Mechanic What it does Challenges Named pieces of real work, each with a rule for what counts Badges A permanent record that you finished one; every badge states its own requirement Levels Rise with total points, and unlock a little more of the product at each rung Leaderboard Off unless you turn it on, and it publishes only what the page says it will

A challenge is a piece of work the product can actually check: fill in every part of your profile, have a role countersigned by the company that employed you, get a forum reply marked as the answer. Each one states the rule it counts by, so there is nothing to guess at.

A badge records that a challenge was finished, with the date it happened. Some badges name the company that countersigned the record behind them. Every badge states its requirement whether or not you hold it — a badge that will not say what it takes is a lottery ticket. Badges are not visible to employers. They are a record of what you did on ClearHire, not a credential.

Levels rise with points, and each rung unlocks something concrete rather than decorative — more resume slots, more verification requests in flight at once. Your level is private unless you turn on the one profile line that shows it.

It is off by default and you have to opt in. When you do, the board publishes your display name as it appears on your public profile, your level, your points and how many roles you have confirmed — the count, not which companies. It never publishes anything you have not made public elsewhere. Every row carries a way to report it and a way to block the person, and the moderation process is written on the page rather than described somewhere else. A rank on it is a rank among the people who chose to be listed, and the page says so; it is not a rank among everyone using ClearHire.

It does not change hiring outcomes. Employers do not see your badges, your level or your rank. It does not decay. No streak, no expiry, nothing removed for inactivity. It is not a requirement. Every core feature works whether or not you look at this at all.

documents.t: Job search in ClearHire is the feature that helps you discover roles posted on the platform and narrow them with filters for location, remote status, salary, and skills, while saving searches and setting alerts so new matches reach you. It pairs with your profile: the skills and experience you record make matching more relevant.

You can refine results by the criteria that matter most: Location — target specific cities or regions. Remote — focus on remote-friendly roles. Salary — filter by pay range where jobs include it. Skills — match roles to the skills on your profile. Combining filters keeps the list focused. The more accurate your profile skills, the more useful skill-based filtering becomes.

When you land on a filter combination that works, save it. A saved search remembers your criteria so you can re-run it in one tap instead of rebuilding filters each visit. This is ideal when you are tracking a niche — for example, "remote, React, senior" — over several weeks.

Job alerts notify you when new roles match a saved search, so you do not have to check back constantly. Alerts turn job search from a chore into a feed: you set the criteria once and ClearHire surfaces fresh matches as they appear.

When you find a role worth pursuing: Review the job details and requirements. Tailor a CV in the resume builder and check it with the ATS checker. Apply, then log it in application tracking so you can follow it from applied to offer. Before you apply, you can request employment verification for past roles. Once a company confirms one, it shows as countersigned on your profile.

It does not aggregate the entire internet. Results reflect jobs available within ClearHire, not every listing everywhere. It does not guarantee matches or interviews. Filters improve relevance; outcomes depend on open roles and employer decisions. It does not auto-apply. You decide where to apply; ClearHire helps you find and track roles.

documents.t: Notifications in ClearHire are the ways the app tells you about activity on your own account — in-app messages inside the product, optional push notifications on your device or browser, and a small set of transactional emails. All three are about your own account activity; none of them are marketing.

In-app notifications appear inside ClearHire and cover your own activity, including: Application status changes as you move through the stages in application tracking. Employment-verification results when an employer confirms a role or a request times out — see employment verification. Reviews tied to your verified employment — see company reviews. Forum replies, messages, follows and endorsements from the community side of the product. System announcements — see below. They are generated as these events happen and are visible whenever you are signed in.

Occasionally ClearHire needs to tell everyone something — a provider outage, a window that has been paused, a change worth knowing about before you notice it yourself. Those arrive as an announcement, which reaches you two ways at once: as an in-app notification, and by email. How loud an announcement is decides how it behaves, and there are three settings: Severity What it does Notice Appears in your notifications and nowhere else Important Raises a band at the top of every page, which you can dismiss Urgent Raises a band you cannot dismiss; it leaves when you open it or when a later announcement replaces it Announcements are sent by ClearHire staff, are recorded in an audit log with the address of whoever sent them, and cannot be recalled once they have gone out — a later announcement can supersede one, but the first is already delivered. They are never marketing: an announcement is about the product working or not working.

Push notifications are optional and off by default. You can turn them on for your device or browser in Notification Settings, and turn them off again at any time. ClearHire works fully without push — it is a convenience for hearing about activity while the app is closed, not a requirement. ClearHire's push is receive-only, and that is worth being precise about. Your device subscribes; what arrives is composed by the ClearHire team rather than generated automatically for every event. So push is a way of hearing about something important while the app is closed — it is not a second copy of every in-app notification, and turning it off costs you nothing you would not also see the next time you open the product.

ClearHire sends a few transactional emails tied to specific actions: Welcome email when you first sign in. Contact-form reply routing when you message the team. Account-deletion confirmation after you delete your account. Identity-verification result when your verification is decided. ClearHire does not send marketing or promotional email, and there is no newsletter.

They do not share your activity with anyone else. Notifications are about your own account. Push is not required. Every feature works whether or not you enable push. Emails are transactional only. No marketing, no newsletter, no selling your address.

documents.t: Profile management in ClearHire is the system that stores your career as structured data across seven sections — experience, education, projects, skills, languages, certifications, and awards — so it can be reused across resumes, job matching, and verification. It replaces the habit of keeping your "real" resume in one document and copy-pasting from it; in ClearHire, the profile is the canonical record and every output is generated from it.

documents.t: Resumes: The resume builder reads your profile and lets you pick which sections and entries to show per job, then exports to PDF or DOCX. documents.t: The ClearHire resume builder is the tool that converts your structured profile into a polished, exportable CV using multiple professional templates, per-section control, and PDF or DOCX output. Because it reads from your profile rather than a separate document, you tailor each resume to a job by choosing what to show — without retyping your history. Most of this generation happens client-side in your browser, so building and exporting is fast and works on the web app and the Android app alike.

ClearHire ships several professional templates covering clean single-column layouts and more visual designs. You can switch between them freely; since content lives in your profile, changing templates simply re-renders the same information. A practical rule: choose a simple, single-column template when a role likely uses an applicant tracking system, and reserve more decorative layouts for creative roles where a human reviews first.

You decide what appears on each resume: Toggle sections on or off (hide Awards or Languages when they are not relevant). Reorder sections so the strongest one leads. Select individual entries to keep a resume focused and within one to two pages. This per-job tailoring is the core advantage of building from a profile: one canonical record, many targeted outputs. For a guided first run, see build your first resume.

The live preview shows page breaks, spacing, and length before you export. Use it to confirm dates align, bullets stay concise, and the layout reads cleanly. Refining here is faster than re-exporting repeatedly.

documents.t: A document-first resume locks your information inside one file's layout. A structured profile keeps each fact as data, which means ClearHire can re-arrange it into different templates, hide or show sections per job, and feed your skills into search filters and the ATS checker. List each role with a clear title, the employer, start and end dates, and a few bullet points focused on outcomes. Strong bullets use action verbs and, where possible, concrete results. This is also the section you can later get verified.
Add your degrees and relevant programs. Include dates so the timeline reads cleanly on a resume.
Use this for work that does not fit neatly under a job: open-source contributions, freelance builds, or portfolio pieces. You can attach links and files, which also feed the portfolio view.

Add the skills that genuinely describe you. These are matched against job requirements in job search and scored against a job description in the ATS resume checker, so accuracy matters more than volume.
These optional sections round out your profile. Include them when they are relevant to the roles you target; leave them out when they add noise.

Start with experience and skills. They drive the most value across resumes, search, and the ATS checker. Write outcome-focused bullets. "Reduced load time 40%" beats "responsible for performance." Keep dates consistent. Gaps and overlaps are easier to explain when the timeline is clear. Update after every role change. A current profile means a current resume on demand. Don't pad. Honest, specific entries outperform long lists of vague claims.

documents.t: The ClearHire ATS resume checker is a tool that compares your resume against a specific job description and shows how well your keywords and content align with what the role asks for. An ATS — applicant tracking system — is the software many employers use to organize and filter applications, and the checker helps you make sure your resume speaks the same language as the job before you apply.

An applicant tracking system stores applications and helps recruiters search and filter them, often by keywords drawn from the job description. It is not a single universal robot that "rejects" resumes; different employers configure their systems differently. The practical takeaway is the same either way: a resume that clearly reflects the role's real requirements is easier for both software and humans to recognize as a match.

You provide two things — your resume content and the target job description — and the checker evaluates how well they align, focusing on the keywords and skills the role emphasizes. Because it runs client-side as part of ClearHire's career tools, your inputs are processed on your device while you work. The output points you to gaps: skills or terms the job stresses that your resume underuses, and areas where your wording could mirror the role more closely.

Add genuinely matching skills. If the job asks for a skill you truly have, make sure it is on your profile and resume. Mirror the role's language where it is accurate — use the job's real terms instead of synonyms it may not search for. Quantify outcomes in your bullets so both software and recruiters see substance. Cut irrelevant content that dilutes the match for this specific role. Re-check after edits to confirm the alignment improved, then export and apply. Avoid keyword stuffing. Cramming in terms you cannot back up reads poorly to humans and does not help you in an interview.

documents.t: Exporting a resume in ClearHire is the step that turns your formatted CV into a downloadable file in either PDF or DOCX format, ready to send to employers or edit elsewhere. The choice between the two is simple once you know what each is for: PDF preserves your layout exactly for applications, and DOCX stays editable for further changes.
documents.s: Export a ClearHire Resume as PDF or DOCX

documents.t: Open the resume builder and select the resume you want. Confirm your template and that the right profile sections are toggled on. Use the live preview to check page breaks, length, and spacing. Choose Export. Pick PDF or DOCX. The file downloads to your device (on Android, it is saved through the native file handling).

Requesting employment verification in ClearHire is the action that asks a former or current employer to confirm a specific role on your profile, which — once confirmed — earns that role a countersignature. This guide walks through sending the request, what the employer sees on their side, and how the timeout works, so you know what to expect at each step. For the concept and what a countersignature does and does not prove, read the employment verification overview first.

Make sure the role exists in your profile with accurate title, employer, and dates. Identify a contact who can actually confirm the role — usually HR or a direct manager. Verify your most important roles first; these are the ones a hiring manager will scrutinize.

Open your profile and select the experience entry you want verified. Choose the option to request verification for that role. Provide the employer or contact details ClearHire needs to route the request. Submit the request. Wait for the employer to act on it (see the timeout below). When confirmed, the role shows as Countersigned.

On the company side, an authorized contact receives your request through ClearHire for companies. They can review the details of the role you have asked them to confirm and then confirm or decline. Confirming acknowledges that the employment relationship existed — it does not ask them to rate your performance or disclose your salary.

The employer-side request has a timeout. If the contact does not act within that window, the request lapses rather than staying open forever. This keeps requests fresh and prevents a pile-up of stale asks. Situation What happens What to do Employer confirms in time Role is countersigned Nothing — you're done Employer declines Role is declined Contact them or pick another contact Request times out Request lapses Send a fresh request A lapsed request is not a rejection and not a black mark. You can simply request again, choose a different contact, or follow up outside the app.

Pick the right person. A contact who can confirm the role avoids a wasted, timed-out request. Give accurate details. Matching title and dates make confirmation easy. Follow up politely. A quick nudge before the window closes can make the difference. Re-request when needed. Timeouts happen; a new request is straightforward.
The request carries a timeout window. If it is not actioned in time, the request lapses and you can send a new one.

documents.t: A reference check asks how you did. ClearHire asks a narrower question: whether you held this title at this company between these dates. A named person there answers from the company’s records, and the answer is kept under their name, with the date. That is a countersignature. It sits beside the role on your profile and on any resume you publish, and it is the one line on the page that somebody other than you signed. The rest of the product is what that line needs around it. A resume builder keeps one profile and cuts a resume per role, with PDF and DOCX out and a public link you can switch off again. Career tools, most of which need no account, cover the application, the interview and the number. Companies get the other side of the same record: post a role, search candidates, run the stages, answer a claim.

documents.t: Three facts, as the company has them: the job title, the company and the dates, confirmed by a named person at the company, with their job title and the date. Either side can start it. You claim a role and the company gets 7 days; a company asks and you get 3. Silence expires the request instead of failing it, so a role with no countersignature is not false. It is unconfirmed, which is where every role starts. It is not a background check. Nobody ran one. It is not an identity check and it is not an endorsement: the company confirmed that you worked there, not that you were good at it. A declined claim stays between you and the company and never appears on a public profile. The whole mechanism, both sides, is on employment verification; the step-by-step is request employment verification.

documents.t: Job seekers build a profile once, cut resumes from it in the resume builder, search jobs, keep every application on a board with 12 stages, and use the career tools, from the ATS check to the salary calculator. Companies keep a company profile, post roles, run applicants through the same 12 stages, search for people, answer claims about roles held with them, and exchange reviews tied to a countersigned record, so feedback comes from people who actually worked together.

On the web at clearhire.aoneahsan.com, and on Android. There is no iOS app, no browser extension (dropped in 2.0, see browser extensions) and no desktop app, because the web app already is one. Sign-in is Google only. There is no ClearHire password, so there is none to reset and none to lose. One account serves both, so a resume started on the web can be finished on the phone.

Three plans: Free, Pro and Team. Every feature is in Free, employment verification included. Free is a plan, not a trial. It does not run out. A paid plan raises a ceiling, never credibility: a record countersigned on Free is identical to one countersigned on a paid plan. Every ceiling is a count. How many saved resumes, how many job alerts, that kind of limit. The current table is on the app’s pricing page. Anything paid is bought on the web; the Android app shows which plan you are on and never sells one. Today the only promotions in the product are cards for the developer’s other apps. An organisation that wants to run its own copy of the platform can license it; every figure for that is on the app’s licensing page, and none of it touches the public app. If ClearHire is useful to you and you want to support it, there is a tip jar at aoneahsan.com/payment.

This ClearHire privacy summary is a plain-language overview of what the app stores, which services it relies on, and the rights you have over your data — written to help you understand the product, not to serve as the legal policy. The authoritative, binding privacy policy lives in the app itself at clearhire.aoneahsan.com/privacy. If anything here differs from that policy, the in-app policy governs.

ClearHire stores the data needed to run the product in a Postgres database on Supabase, including: Your profile: experience, education, projects, skills, languages, certifications, awards Resumes you build and related settings Applications you track and their stages Reviews tied to verified employment Verification requests and confirmations Files you upload (for projects or portfolio) are stored in FilesHub rather than in the database. ClearHire also keeps aggregate profile-view counts. For signed-out visitors, view counting uses a per-day identifier to avoid double-counting and does not build a personal profile of the viewer.

To operate, ClearHire relies on a small set of providers: Provider Purpose Supabase The database, authentication, and the server functions the app runs on Google Analytics 4 Product analytics Amplitude Product analytics Microsoft Clarity Product and usage insight Sentry Error monitoring OneSignal Push notifications, if you turn them on FilesHub Storage for uploaded files and transactional email delivery This list is kept in step with the provider table in the in-app privacy policy, which is the binding one. If the two ever disagree, that policy is right and this page is out of date. ClearHire sends a small number of transactional emails through FilesHub — welcome, contact-form reply, account-deletion confirmation, and identity-verification result. It sends no marketing email. See notifications and emails. These help the app function, understand usage, and stay reliable. ClearHire does not use third-party advertising networks; the only promotions shown are first-party ads for the developer's other apps.

Employment verification involves two parties: you and the employer you ask. When you request verification, ClearHire shares only what is necessary for that employer to confirm the role. The confirmation result (the verified status of the role) is then reflected for you. Verification is about confirming a relationship, not exposing unrelated personal data.

ClearHire shows promotions for the developer's other apps only — including a promo card that opens shortly after launch. There are no third-party ad networks, which means your data is not sold or shared to power external ad targeting. Be aware that the analytics providers listed above still run regardless of the promotions: Microsoft Clarity in particular records usage sessions. There is no in-app toggle to switch product analytics off.

You can take your data with you and remove it: Export your resumes as PDF or DOCX and keep copies of key details. Delete your account and data through the in-app account-deletion flow. Step-by-step instructions are in data export and deletion.
